america-colonies.prompt: For centuries, people assumed the original Jamestown fort had washed away. What happened in 1994?
options: An archaeologist dug where he thought it should be and found the fort's wall within weeks
A flood revealed the fort's remains naturally
Colonial records were found describing its exact location
america-colonies.explain: They've since dug up armor, tools, coins, and graves of the first settlers, all inside those walls.

america-colonies.prompt: Where did the log cabin — often thought of as a classic American idea — actually come from?
options: Swedish and Finnish settlers, for whom stacking logs was already ordinary at home
English colonists who adapted their timber-frame style
Native American building techniques
america-colonies.explain: English colonists actually built timber-frame houses with sawn boards — log cabins spread because they needed only an axe and trees.

america-colonies.prompt: Benjamin Franklin got his writing published in his brother's newspaper by pretending to be a middle-aged widow.
america-colonies.explain: He slid the letters under the door at night under a false name, since he wasn't allowed to write for the paper himself.

america-founding.prompt: Why are the signatures on the Declaration of Independence so faded today, except John Hancock's?
options: Years of display in sunlight damaged most signatures, though Hancock's stayed clearest
The ink used was naturally unstable
It was copied poorly from the original
america-founding.explain: That's actually why 'John Hancock' became slang for a signature.

america-founding.prompt: What makes Jefferson's rough draft of the Declaration unusual among famous historical documents?
options: It still has the crossings-out on it, showing exactly what was argued over and cut
It's the only copy that still exists
It was written in a code that took centuries to decipher
america-founding.explain: You can see which words were debated before reaching the final version — an unusual thing to have for any famous document.

america-founding.prompt: George Washington's famous false teeth were actually made of wood.
america-founding.explain: The surviving set is made of hippopotamus ivory, human teeth, brass screws, and a lead base — they just stained dark over time.

america-inventors.prompt: What do Edison's roughly five million pages of notebooks mostly contain?
options: Failures — sketches, dead ends, and lists of things tried and crossed off
Finished diagrams of his successful inventions
Personal letters and business records
america-inventors.explain: Hundreds of filament materials were tested for the light bulb alone, one after another, each written down.

america-inventors.prompt: How did Elisha Otis prove his elevator safety brake actually worked, in 1854?
options: He stood on a platform hoisted above a crowd and had an assistant cut the rope with an axe
He wrote a detailed mathematical paper on the physics involved
He demonstrated it privately to investors only
america-inventors.explain: The brake caught as designed — tall buildings only became worth building once people trusted elevators enough to use them.

america-inventors.prompt: George Washington Carver is credited with inventing peanut butter.
america-inventors.explain: Peanut butter already existed — what he actually did was find hundreds of uses for peanuts, persuading farmers to grow them to help restore soil cotton had stripped.

america-frontier.prompt: How did wagon wheels carve a groove up to 5 feet deep into solid rock along the Oregon Trail?
options: So many iron-tyred wheels crossed the same soft sandstone ridge, one wagon at a time, over years
Workers deliberately carved the groove to mark the trail
A flash flood eroded the rock quickly
america-frontier.explain: Nobody dug it — it was worn down by wheels, one wagon at a time.

america-frontier.prompt: Why did the famous Pony Express only last eighteen months?
options: The telegraph reached the coast and made it pointless overnight
It ran out of money too quickly to continue
Too many riders quit the dangerous job
america-frontier.explain: It was famous immediately but never made money — it's remembered out of all proportion to how long it actually existed.

america-frontier.prompt: On the treeless plains, settlers built houses out of strips of cut turf, stacked like bricks.
america-frontier.explain: The walls were about 2 feet thick — warm in winter, but known to leak mud when it rained.

america-machines.prompt: How did the whole country learn instantly when the transcontinental railroad was completed in 1869?
options: A telegraph wire was attached to the ceremonial hammer and last spike, sending a signal the moment it struck
Newspapers had reporters stationed at the site to telegraph the news
Church bells were rung in a relay across the country
america-machines.explain: The man swinging the hammer actually missed on his first try, but the telegraph operator sent the signal anyway.

america-machines.prompt: What was Henry Ford's actual key innovation with the assembly line?
options: He moved the factory past the car instead of having workers move around a stationary car
He invented the automobile engine
He was the first to use steel instead of iron in car frames
america-machines.explain: Building one chassis went from twelve and a half hours to just ninety-three minutes — the idea partly came from meat-packing plants.

america-machines.prompt: Before 1883, every American town set its own clock by the sun, making railroad scheduling nearly impossible.
america-machines.explain: The railroads simply invented four time zones and imposed them — the government didn't make it official law for another 35 years.

america-flight.prompt: How did the Wright brothers solve the problem of published wing-performance tables giving them the wrong results?
options: They built their own wind tunnel out of a wooden box and a fan, and tested about 200 wing shapes themselves
They hired mathematicians to recalculate the existing tables
They copied designs from European inventors instead
america-flight.explain: The published tables really were wrong — everyone else had been designing from them anyway.

america-flight.prompt: What was the Wright brothers' real breakthrough invention, more than the wing or the engine itself?
options: Control — twisting the wing to roll the aircraft, inspired by watching a buzzard tilt
A lightweight, powerful engine
A way to launch the aircraft without a runway
america-flight.explain: They worked the wing twist and rudder together with one coordinated movement.

america-flight.prompt: The Wright brothers' famous 1903 flight could barely get off the ground, and their real breakthrough aircraft came two years later.
america-flight.explain: Their 1905 machine, Flyer III, stayed up for 39 minutes and circled a field 30 times — almost nobody can name it.

america-everyday.prompt: Before refrigeration existed, how did people get ice, even in places far from any cold climate?
options: Men cut it from frozen New England ponds and shipped it as far as India, packed in sawdust
It was manufactured using early refrigeration machines
It was imported from northern countries by rail
america-everyday.explain: Everyone told Frederic Tudor the idea was ridiculous, and his first cargo mostly melted — but it eventually made his fortune.

america-everyday.prompt: What was unusual about how some Americans got their houses in the early 1900s?
options: You could order one by mail, and it arrived as 30,000 numbered pieces to assemble yourself
Houses were built entirely by local co-ops for free
Pre-built houses were shipped whole by train
america-everyday.explain: Thousands of these mail-order houses are still standing, and people still live in them today.

america-everyday.prompt: By 1935, electricity had already reached most American farms, just like it had reached cities decades earlier.
america-everyday.explain: Only about one farm in ten had electricity in 1935 — running lines to scattered farms cost more than companies could profit from, so farmers formed their own co-ops.

ancient-beginning.prompt: How did Archbishop James Ussher arrive at his famous 4004 BC date for creation?
options: He added up the ages given in the Genesis family lists
The date is stated directly in the Bible
He used carbon dating on ancient artifacts
ancient-beginning.explain: Nowhere does the Bible state 4004 BC directly — that number is arithmetic Ussher did on the genealogies, published in 1650.

ancient-beginning.prompt: Why do some people land on a creation date nearer 5500 BC instead of Ussher's 4004 BC?
options: Older copies of Genesis, like the Greek Septuagint, give longer gaps in the same family lists
They used a completely different method than adding genealogies
Scientists have disproven Ussher's calculation
ancient-beginning.explain: Both totals are honest arithmetic on a written list — they differ because the lists themselves differ.

ancient-beginning.prompt: What makes the Genesis 5 and 11 genealogies unusual compared to most ancient writing?
options: They actually record how many years passed between one person and the next
They list far more people than other ancient texts
They were written in a unique script
ancient-beginning.explain: That detail is exactly why building a timeline from them is possible at all — most ancient writing doesn't give that information.

ancient-beginning.prompt: The oldest known fragment of Bible text is a full scroll, carefully preserved on parchment.
ancient-beginning.explain: It's actually two tiny rolled silver strips, small enough to fit in your palm, found in a Jerusalem burial cave.

ancient-flood.prompt: What is the "Flood Tablet" in the British Museum, and how is its flood story different from Genesis?
options: A Babylonian account with different names, gods, and boat details, but clearly about the same kind of event
An exact copy of the Genesis flood account in a different language
A tablet that disproves the Genesis flood story
ancient-flood.explain: It's part of the Babylonian Epic of Gilgamesh, dug up at Nineveh.

ancient-flood.prompt: What's one specific detail in the Genesis account of the Tower of Babel that matches what we know about ancient southern Iraq?
options: The tower was described as built of brick and tar, since that region has almost no building stone
The tower's exact height is given in cubits
The language spoken there is named directly
ancient-flood.explain: That detail about brick only matters if you know the region — and it checks out.

ancient-flood.prompt: Flood stories only appear in the written traditions of cultures that had contact with each other near the Middle East.
ancient-flood.explain: They turn up in Babylon, Greece, India, China, and peoples across the Americas and Pacific — many of whom had no contact with each other.

ancient-egypt.prompt: What's actually the most astonishing part of the Great Pyramid, according to the people who've measured it?
options: The precision — its four sides differ in length by less than 8 inches, on a 13-acre base
Its sheer size compared to other ancient buildings
How quickly it was reportedly built
ancient-egypt.explain: The ground it sits on was leveled to within about an inch across the whole structure.

ancient-egypt.prompt: How do historians actually arrive at 2560 BC as the Great Pyramid's construction date?
options: By combining Egyptian king-lists with carbon dates from its mortar
It's carved directly into the pyramid's stone
Ancient Egyptian calendars state it exactly
ancient-egypt.explain: Nothing on the pyramid gives a year — that date, like any ancient date, is worked out, not read off the stone.

ancient-egypt.prompt: How did the Rosetta Stone help scholars finally read Egyptian hieroglyphs?
options: The same decree was carved on it in three scripts, one of which (Greek) people could still read
It was the first hieroglyphic text ever discovered
It contained a translation guide written by ancient Egyptian scholars
ancient-egypt.explain: Jean-François Champollion announced he'd cracked the code in 1822, after finding a king's name inside an oval cartouche.

ancient-egypt.prompt: Hieroglyphs are mostly picture-writing, where each symbol represents the object it looks like.
ancient-egypt.explain: Most hieroglyphic signs actually stand for sounds, not things — which is how Champollion cracked them by looking for a specific name.

options: Pressing a cut reed into wet clay leaves a wedge-shaped mark
The clay tablets themselves were shaped like wedges
Scribes used wedge-shaped tools to carve stone
ancient-mesopot.explain: Cuneiform comes from Latin for wedge-shaped — hundreds of thousands of these tablets have been dug up.

ancient-mesopot.prompt: What does the Code of Hammurabi, now in the Louvre, actually contain?
options: 282 laws covering things like farm rent, wages, and what happens if a house collapses
A record of Hammurabi's military victories
A genealogy of Babylonian kings
ancient-mesopot.explain: It's one of the oldest legal documents anyone can still read, and it wasn't even found in Babylon — it turned up in Iran as loot.

ancient-mesopot.prompt: A king's library discovered at Nineveh survived mostly because the palace it was in burned down.
ancient-mesopot.explain: Fire destroys paper and parchment, but it actually bakes clay tablets harder — the library survived because it was destroyed.

ancient-israel.prompt: What did the Tel Dan inscription, found in 1993, actually prove about King David?
options: It's the earliest mention of David found outside the Bible, countering claims he was purely legendary
It gives the exact dates of David's reign
It was written by David himself
ancient-israel.explain: The broken basalt stone names the 'House of David' in a king's boast about his victories.

ancient-israel.prompt: What's remarkable about the 1,750-foot tunnel still carrying water under Jerusalem?
options: Two teams cut it from opposite ends through solid rock, and their paths actually met
It was built using machines far ahead of its time
It was discovered completely by accident in modern times
ancient-israel.explain: The tunnel's S-shaped path and changing pick marks show exactly where the two digging teams met.

ancient-israel.prompt: What did the 1947 discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls near a cave actually show about the Bible?
options: The text had been copied for a very long time with remarkably few changes
The biblical text had changed significantly over the centuries
The scrolls contained entirely unknown books of the Bible
ancient-israel.explain: One scroll is a complete, 24-foot-long book of Isaiah — found when a shepherd's thrown stone broke pottery in a cave.

ancient-israel.prompt: The Cyrus Cylinder, found at Babylon, describes Cyrus sending captured peoples back to their homelands to rebuild their temples.
ancient-israel.explain: That matches the same policy described in the book of Ezra, even though the cylinder doesn't name Judah specifically.

ancient-greece.prompt: What did sponge divers accidentally discover in a 1901 shipwreck off Antikythera?
options: A corroded device with at least 30 meshed bronze gears that tracked the sun, moon, and eclipses
A cache of ancient Greek coins
A collection of bronze statues
ancient-greece.explain: Nothing else of that mechanical complexity survives from anywhere near its time.

ancient-greece.prompt: What did the Greeks add to the alphabet they borrowed from the Phoenicians?
options: Vowels
Punctuation marks
Numbers
ancient-greece.explain: Our letters A, B, and E are those same Greek letters, handed down through the Romans.

ancient-greece.prompt: The famous story of a runner dying after carrying news of victory from Marathon to Athens comes from the earliest written account of the battle.
ancient-greece.explain: Herodotus, who wrote closest to the event, actually describes a runner going the opposite direction, to Sparta, to ask for help.

ancient-rome.prompt: Why do ancient Roman concrete harbors still stand strong in seawater today, while modern concrete would crumble?
options: Seawater reacts with volcanic ash mixed into the concrete, growing new crystals that make it stronger over time
Roman engineers used a secret ingredient that's since been lost forever
Roman concrete was never actually exposed to seawater
ancient-rome.explain: This was discovered by drilling cores out of Roman harbors and studying them under microscopes — the recipe was written down by Vitruvius; it just stopped being used.

ancient-rome.prompt: How did the Romans survey a 31-mile aqueduct so precisely that it drops only 41 feet over its entire length?
options: With water levels and sighting rods
Using mathematical formulas we no longer understand
They didn't — the slope was mostly accidental
ancient-rome.explain: Too steep and the water would tear the channel apart; too flat and it would stop — the Pont du Gard bridge that carries it is still standing.

ancient-rome.prompt: At Pompeii, pouring plaster into holes in hardened volcanic ash reveals the actual shape of a person's body at their last moment.
ancient-rome.explain: The bodies decayed away, leaving holes exactly their shape — pouring plaster in captures that shape when it hardens.

america-explorers.prompt: How did a Norwegian couple find a real Norse settlement in Newfoundland in 1960?
options: They read old Viking sagas describing a place called Vinland and took the descriptions as directions
They found it using ground-penetrating radar
Local Indigenous people showed them the site
america-explorers.explain: Most people had assumed the sagas describing Vinland were just stories — the Ingstads took them literally.

america-explorers.prompt: During the Lewis and Clark expedition, who saved the expedition's instruments, books, and papers when a boat tipped over?
options: Sacagawea
Meriwether Lewis
William Clark
america-explorers.explain: She did this while traveling the entire route with a baby son on her back — Clark later named a river after her.

america-explorers.prompt: Why did sailors need an extremely accurate clock to figure out how far east or west they'd traveled?
options: They had to compare their local noon with the time at a known location
Clocks were needed to track how many days they'd been sailing
An accurate clock helped them read star positions
america-explorers.explain: Figuring out north-south position was easy — just measure the sun at noon — but east-west required comparing times.

astro-sun.prompt: Why is it so dangerous to stare at the sun, even though it doesn't hurt at the time?
options: The retina has no pain nerves, so damage happens with no warning
The sun's light is too dim to notice damage
Sunglasses already block all the dangerous light
astro-sun.explain: There's no treatment for the damage, called solar retinopathy — and sunglasses are nowhere near dark enough.

astro-sun.prompt: How did scientists first discover the element helium, before it was ever found on Earth?
options: An unexplained yellow line showed up in sunlight during a solar eclipse
A volcanic eruption released it into the air
It was found inside a meteorite
astro-sun.explain: Jules Janssen spotted it in 1868; it wasn't found on Earth, in volcanic gas, until 1882.

astro-sun.prompt: How do scientists know the sun's center is about 27 million degrees, if nobody has ever been inside it?
options: They work it out from how the sun rings and wobbles, plus what its light contains
A probe has flown through the sun's core
It's measured the same way as the surface temperature
astro-sun.explain: The surface temperature (about 10,000°F) is measured directly; the core figure is reasoned out, like telling a cracked bell from a whole one by its sound.

astro-sun.prompt: In 1859, a solar flare was strong enough to make telegraph wires spark across Europe and North America.
astro-sun.explain: That's the Carrington Event — some operators unhooked their batteries and kept sending messages on the current the sky was pushing through the wires.

astro-sun.prompt: A sunspot looks black because it's actually much colder than the rest of the sun.
astro-sun.explain: It's not cold at all — about 6,300°F. It just looks dark next to the surface around it, which is roughly 10,000°F.

astro-moon.prompt: How much of the moon's surface have people actually been able to see from Earth, counting its slight wobble?
options: About 59 percent
Exactly half
Nearly 100 percent
astro-moon.explain: The wobble, called libration, lets us peek a little around each edge over time.

astro-moon.prompt: How do scientists know the moon is drifting away from Earth, a tiny bit every year?
options: Lasers are bounced off mirrors astronauts left on the surface, and the round-trip is timed
Telescopes measure its size getting smaller
Its orbit has been recalculated using new math
astro-moon.explain: The measurement is good to a few millimeters — the moon drifts about 1.5 inches farther away each year.

astro-moon.prompt: Without wind, rain, or water, why are Apollo astronauts' bootprints still on the moon today?
options: Nothing on the moon can sweep them away except very slow dust from tiny impacts
Special material was sprayed on the ground to preserve them
They were photographed and then physically protected
astro-moon.explain: Orbiting cameras have photographed the landing sites, and the tracks the crews walked and drove still show up.

astro-moon.prompt: The far side of the moon is actually called the "dark side" because it never gets any sunlight.
astro-moon.explain: It gets just as much sunlight as the near side — it simply never faces Earth.

astro-moon.prompt: The best time to see craters clearly on the moon is during a full moon.
astro-moon.explain: At full moon the sun is overhead with no shadows; craters show up best along the line between lit and unlit ground.

astro-rocky.prompt: Mercury is closest to the sun, so why isn't it the hottest planet?
options: Venus's thick carbon-dioxide air traps heat, even though it's farther from the sun
Mercury is actually farther from the sun than it appears
Venus is closer to the sun than Mercury
astro-rocky.explain: Venus runs about 870°F — hot enough to melt lead — because of its thick, heat-trapping atmosphere.

astro-rocky.prompt: Why would a sunset on Venus actually rise in the west instead of the east?
options: Venus spins backward, and its day is even longer than its year
Venus doesn't rotate at all
Venus orbits the sun in the opposite direction
astro-rocky.explain: One Venus rotation takes 243 Earth days; one trip around the sun takes only 225.

astro-rocky.prompt: How do scientists know what's inside Earth's core, since nobody has ever drilled anywhere near it?
options: They study where certain earthquake waves simply never arrive on the far side of the planet
Deep-sea submarines have reached the core
It's measured the same way ocean depth is measured
astro-rocky.explain: That gap in the readings — a shadow certain waves can't cross — is the evidence pointing to a liquid outer core.

astro-rocky.prompt: A 70-pound kid would weigh less on Mars because its gravity is weaker than Earth's.
astro-rocky.explain: Mars's gravity is about 38 percent of Earth's, so that same kid would weigh about 26 pounds there.

astro-rocky.prompt: Mercury is the smallest object in the solar system that people call a planet.
astro-rocky.explain: Two moons — Ganymede and Titan — are actually wider than Mercury, but they orbit planets instead of the sun.

astro-giants.prompt: What's unusual about Saturn, compared to every other planet?
options: It's the only planet less dense than water — it would float in a big enough ocean
It's the only planet with rings
It's the only planet that spins backward
astro-giants.explain: Its average density is 0.69 grams per cubic centimeter; water is 1.

astro-giants.prompt: How was Neptune actually discovered, before anyone pointed a telescope at it?
options: A mathematician calculated where an unseen planet must be, from how it tugged on Uranus
It was spotted by accident during a routine sky survey
A probe detected its gravity from a distance
astro-giants.explain: Urbain Le Verrier did the math; Johann Galle then found Neptune within one degree of the predicted spot.

astro-giants.prompt: How do scientists think Europa has a hidden ocean under its ice, without ever drilling through?
options: Something under the ice bends Jupiter's magnetic field in a way that fits a salty ocean
A probe has already landed and confirmed it directly
Telescopes can see through the ice to the water below
astro-giants.explain: It's a conclusion drawn from a magnetic reading and the pattern of cracks — never actually observed.

astro-giants.prompt: Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been shrinking since the 1800s, which scientists have actually measured over time.
astro-giants.explain: In 1879 it measured about 24,000 miles across; Hubble now measures it at about 10,250 miles.

astro-giants.prompt: Cassini was deliberately crashed into Saturn's atmosphere so it could never accidentally contaminate one of Saturn's moons.
astro-giants.explain: It burned up on purpose on September 15, 2017, so it could never carry Earth bacteria onto a moon worth protecting.

astro-smallstuff.prompt: Movies show the asteroid belt as a crowded obstacle course. What's it really like?
options: Mostly empty — asteroids average about 600,000 miles apart
Just as crowded as the movies show
Dense enough that spacecraft must carefully steer around rocks
astro-smallstuff.explain: That's more than twice the Earth-moon distance — spacecraft fly straight through without steering around anything.

astro-smallstuff.prompt: Why does a comet's tail always point away from the sun, no matter which direction the comet is moving?
options: Sunlight and the solar wind push the dust and gas straight outward
The tail is just smoke trailing behind it like a train
Gravity pulls the tail away from the sun
astro-smallstuff.explain: A comet heading back out of the solar system actually travels tail-first.

astro-smallstuff.prompt: Why was Pluto reclassified as a "dwarf planet" in 2006?
options: It hasn't cleared its own orbital neighborhood of other similar-sized objects
It turned out to be much smaller than first thought
It doesn't orbit the sun
astro-smallstuff.explain: Pluto shares its region of the solar system with Eris and other bodies of similar size — nothing about Pluto itself changed, the definition did.

astro-smallstuff.prompt: The largest meteorite ever found, in Namibia, is still lying exactly where it landed because no one can move it.
astro-smallstuff.explain: Hoba weighs over 60 tons — a farmer's plow struck it in 1920, and it's never been moved since.

astro-smallstuff.prompt: Edmond Halley actually lived to see his famous comet return in 1758, just as he predicted.
astro-smallstuff.explain: It arrived sixteen years after he died — he predicted it decades in advance.

astro-stars.prompt: What does a star's color actually tell you?
options: How hot its surface is — blue is hotter, red is cooler
How far away it is
How old the star is
astro-stars.explain: The same way a poker in a fire goes from dull red to orange to white as it heats up.

astro-stars.prompt: What's the simplest trick for telling a planet from a star in the night sky?
options: Planets don't twinkle the way stars do
Planets are always brighter than stars
Stars only appear in winter
astro-stars.explain: A star arrives as a single point of light that wobbles in the air; a planet arrives as a tiny disc, and the wobbles cancel out.

astro-stars.prompt: How is the distance to a nearby star actually measured?
options: Parallax — watching how the star appears to shift as Earth orbits the sun
By measuring how bright the star looks
By timing how long its light takes to arrive
astro-stars.explain: It's the same trick as holding up a finger and closing one eye, then the other — Earth's two eyes are its position in January and July.

astro-stars.prompt: The three stars in Orion's belt are actually close neighbors to each other in space.
astro-stars.explain: They only look evenly spaced from here — Alnitak sits around 1,260 light-years away, Alnilam nearly 2,000.

astro-stars.prompt: A deaf teenager figured out why the star Algol dims and brightens every few days, by carefully timing it.
astro-stars.explain: John Goodricke worked out in 1783 that a second star was passing in front of the first — he was 18 at the time.

astro-deepsky.prompt: The Orion Nebula is called a "stellar nursery" because people think stars form there. What has actually been observed happening?
options: Nobody has ever watched a star form inside it
Multiple stars have been filmed forming
Only the birth of planets, not stars
astro-deepsky.explain: The nebula's distance (1,344 light-years) has been measured by parallax — but no one has watched what's happening inside it.

astro-deepsky.prompt: Why do photographs of nebulae show vivid color, while looking through a telescope shows only gray?
options: The eye's dark-adapted sensors can't see color at all, but a camera can collect light for hours
Telescopes remove the color on purpose
The colors only appear in deep space, not through glass
astro-deepsky.explain: A camera can sit collecting light for an hour; your eye resets roughly every tenth of a second.

astro-deepsky.prompt: Why does the Milky Way look like a band across the sky instead of the spiral shape we see in photos of other galaxies?
options: We're inside it, looking along its flat disk from within
It only forms a band during certain seasons
Clouds block the rest of its shape
astro-deepsky.explain: Galileo settled what it was made of in 1610, pointing a telescope at it and watching the glow break into separate stars.

astro-deepsky.prompt: When Hubble stared at an apparently empty patch of sky for ten days in 1995, it found nothing there.
astro-deepsky.explain: That 'empty' patch came back with roughly 3,000 galaxies in it.

astro-deepsky.prompt: The Pleiades star cluster actually has more than a thousand stars in it, even though most people only see six or seven.
astro-deepsky.explain: Binoculars turn those six or seven visible stars into dozens — the full cluster holds over a thousand.

astro-looking.prompt: What is a telescope's real job — the thing that actually makes it powerful?
options: Collecting far more light than your eye can on its own
Magnifying objects to look bigger
Removing the atmosphere's blur completely
astro-looking.explain: A 6-inch mirror gathers around 500 times as much light as a dark-adapted pupil — magnification is a separate, much less important setting.

astro-looking.prompt: Why are major observatories built in miserable, remote places like mountaintops and deserts?
options: They need still, dry, dark air, which convenient places don't have
It's cheaper to build there
Telescopes work better at high altitude regardless of air quality
astro-looking.explain: Water vapor soaks up infrared light, and height gets a telescope above most of the atmosphere's turbulence.

astro-looking.prompt: How do the Keck telescopes' mirrors correct for the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere?
options: A flexible mirror bends hundreds of times a second to cancel out the blur
They're placed in outer space, away from the atmosphere
A computer edits the blur out of photos afterward
astro-looking.explain: They fire a laser to create an artificial star, watch how it wobbles, and bend the mirror to cancel the wobble out.

astro-looking.prompt: When Hubble launched in 1990, its mirror had been ground to the wrong shape, making every picture come back blurry.
astro-looking.explain: The edge was off by about four microns — a fiftieth the thickness of a hair — fixed by astronauts in 1993.

astro-looking.prompt: The very first thing William Herschel reported after discovering Uranus in 1781 was that he'd found a new planet.
astro-looking.explain: He first reported it as a comet — it turned out to be the first planet ever found with a telescope.

body-brain.prompt: What's actually causing "brain freeze" when you eat something very cold too fast?
options: A blood vessel in the roof of your mouth overreacts, and your brain misreads where the signal comes from
Your brain itself is briefly cooled down
Nerves in your teeth send a false pain signal
body-brain.explain: Your brain never actually cools that fast — that's why you feel it in your forehead instead of the roof of your mouth.

body-brain.prompt: Why do London taxi drivers who pass their famously hard 25,000-street test have a measurably larger hippocampus?
options: The brain region they use most while learning actually grows with the work
They're born with larger brains to begin with
It's an illusion from how brain scans are measured
body-brain.explain: Trainees who studied for years but failed the test showed no such growth — the parts you work hardest are the parts that get built up.

body-brain.prompt: People only use about 10 percent of their brain, with the rest sitting unused.
body-brain.explain: Brain scans show activity all over it — damage to almost any small patch costs something, a word, a memory, or a movement.

body-brain.prompt: For decades, textbooks claimed the human brain has 100 billion neurons, but a careful recount found a different number.
body-brain.explain: Suzana Herculano-Houzel dissolved brains into a soup and counted the nuclei — the real number came out near 86 billion.

body-heart.prompt: How did William Harvey prove in 1628 that blood circulates in a loop, without ever seeing a capillary?
options: He calculated that the heart pushes far more blood in half an hour than the whole body could possibly hold
He dissected hundreds of hearts to trace the vessels directly
He used an early microscope to watch blood flow
body-heart.explain: Before Harvey, blood was thought to be made fresh in the liver and used up at the edges — his arithmetic left no other answer.

body-heart.prompt: Why do veins look blue through your skin, even though blood is never actually blue?
options: Blue light bounces back off skin fibers, while red light gets absorbed deep by the dark blood
Veins contain a different, bluer type of blood than arteries
Oxygen turns blood blue once it leaves the lungs
body-heart.explain: The vein itself is red — it's the picture reaching your eye that's blue.

body-heart.prompt: Your heart needs signals from your brain to keep beating in rhythm.
body-heart.explain: A patch of cells at the top of the heart sets its own beat — even single heart cells in a dish will keep beating on their own, which is why a donated heart starts up again in a new chest.

body-bones.prompt: You were born with about 300 bones but now have only 206. What happened to the rest?
options: Some of them fused together as you grew
You lost them through natural wear
They dissolved and were absorbed by your body
body-bones.explain: A baby's skull starts as several separate plates, which is what lets the head flex during birth, then knits together over the first couple of years.

body-bones.prompt: What did Donald Unger prove by cracking only his left hand's knuckles for over 60 years?
options: Cracking knuckles does not cause arthritis
Cracking knuckles makes joints weaker over time
Knuckle cracking sound comes from bone friction
body-bones.explain: X-rays of both his hands showed no difference — he won an Ig Nobel Prize for the experiment in 2009.

body-bones.prompt: Bone is a fixed, unchanging material once you stop growing.
body-bones.explain: Bone is constantly being torn down and rebuilt — over about ten years, your entire skeleton gets replaced.

body-lungs.prompt: If you could unfold the inside surface of your lungs flat, how much space would it cover?
options: A good chunk of a tennis court
About the size of a bedsheet
Roughly the size of your own skin
body-lungs.explain: All that area is folded into your chest as hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs, each thinner than tissue paper.

body-lungs.prompt: A 1959 researcher named Mary Ellen Avery discovered why premature babies sometimes struggle to breathe. What was the cause?
options: Their lungs' air sacs hadn't yet made the soapy film that keeps them from sticking shut when wet
Their lungs were simply too small to hold enough air
Their diaphragm muscles hadn't developed yet
body-lungs.explain: That coating can now be given to premature babies as medicine.

body-lungs.prompt: A 1980s study found that breathing pure oxygen made people yawn less, proving yawning is about getting more oxygen.
body-lungs.explain: Researcher Robert Provine found that neither pure oxygen nor extra carbon dioxide changed how much people yawned — why we yawn is still an open question.

body-senses.prompt: The classic "tongue map" showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back — is it accurate?
options: No — every part of the tongue can actually detect every taste
Yes — it's confirmed by modern taste research
It's accurate only for bitter and sour tastes
body-senses.explain: The diagram came from a mistranslation of a German study and got copied into textbooks for decades.

body-senses.prompt: What's the real explanation for motion sickness in a moving car?
options: Your eyes report stillness while your inner ear reports movement, and your brain can't resolve the conflict
Your stomach is upset by the car's vibrations
Your eyes simply can't process fast-moving scenery
body-senses.explain: Reading in a moving car creates exactly this contradiction, which is why it makes motion sickness worse.

body-senses.prompt: Your nose has enough different smell detectors — one for every smell you can recognize.
body-senses.explain: Your nose has only about 400 types of detector, far fewer than the smells you can tell apart — each smell is actually a pattern across many detectors at once.

body-gut.prompt: How did a doctor named William Beaumont first learn how digestion actually works, in the 1820s?
options: He lowered food on a string into a hole in a patient's stomach that never fully healed after a gunshot wound
He studied cadavers to observe stomach tissue
He experimented on animals and compared results to humans
body-gut.explain: Over 250 experiments on Alexis St. Martin showed that a stomach works by chemistry, not grinding.

body-gut.prompt: Why can astronauts eat and drink normally while floating in zero gravity?
options: Swallowing works by muscles squeezing food along in a wave, not by gravity pulling it down
Food is specially processed to float directly into the stomach
Their stomachs adapt to function without gravity
body-gut.explain: That wave, called peristalsis, means you could technically swallow upside down.

body-gut.prompt: A rumbling stomach is a signal from your body that it urgently needs food.
body-gut.explain: About every 90 minutes, a cleanup wave sweeps through your gut clearing out leftovers — the rumble is just gas and liquid being pushed along, whether or not you're hungry.

body-skin.prompt: Why do your fingers actually wrinkle in the bath?
options: Your nervous system deliberately narrows blood vessels to pull the skin into ridges that grip better wet
Water physically soaks into and swells the skin
Soap chemically reacts with the outer skin layer
body-skin.explain: Nobody has caught the ridges doing their job directly, but the tire-tread pattern is strong evidence they help with grip.

body-skin.prompt: A 1928 study, and every careful one since, tested a common claim about shaving. What did they find?
options: Shaving does not make hair grow back thicker, darker, or faster
Shaving actually slows hair growth over time
Shaving makes hair grow back finer
body-skin.explain: A shaved hair just gets cut flat instead of tapering to a point — that blunt end feels and looks different, but it's the same hair.

body-skin.prompt: You lose most of your body heat through your head, which is why it's especially important to cover it in cold weather.
body-skin.explain: Your head is about a tenth of your skin and loses about a tenth of your heat — the myth traces back to a test where only volunteers' heads were left uncovered.

body-defence.prompt: Why does your body deliberately raise its own temperature when you get a fever?
options: Many germs grow best at normal body temperature, and your immune cells work faster when it's warmer
It's an uncontrolled side effect of fighting infection
Fever helps you sweat out the infection faster
body-defence.explain: A fever is your body turning up the heat on purpose, not damage being done.

body-defence.prompt: What does green snot actually indicate about an illness?
options: Nothing specific — the color comes from an enzyme in white blood cells, whether it's a virus or bacteria
That antibiotics are definitely needed
That the infection has become more serious
body-defence.explain: Green snot shows up regardless of whether the cause is viral or bacterial.

body-defence.prompt: Alexander Fleming discovered a germ-killer in his own tears years before he discovered penicillin.
body-defence.explain: He named it lysozyme in 1922, six years before the mold that led to penicillin — he had volunteers squeeze lemon peel to make their eyes water for testing.

body-sleep.prompt: What did Michel Siffre discover about his own body clock after spending two months alone in a cave with no daylight?
options: His sleep-wake rhythm settled into a day slightly longer than 24 hours, but his sense of time drifted badly
His body clock stopped working entirely without sunlight
He needed far less sleep than normal
body-sleep.explain: When told the two months were up, he thought about a month less had passed — his body kept decent time, but his mind lost track completely.

body-sleep.prompt: Why does a teenager often feel wide awake at 11pm when a younger child would already be asleep?
options: Melatonin, the hormone signaling nighttime, actually rises one to two hours later in a teenager's body
Teenagers simply have more energy than younger children
It's purely a habit, not a biological difference
body-sleep.explain: A teenager still awake late is following their own body clock, not fighting it.

body-sleep.prompt: Overnight, your brain actually flushes out waste that builds up during the day, more strongly than it does while you're awake.
body-sleep.explain: This was first traced in mice using dye — among the waste cleared out are proteins linked to dementia when they build up.

body-cells.prompt: Why does a skin cell hold the complete instructions for building a heart, but never use them?
options: Every cell carries the whole genetic instruction book but only reads its own relevant chapter
Only certain specialized cells carry the full instructions
Heart-building instructions are deleted from skin cells before birth
body-cells.explain: A code that stores, copies, and checks its own spelling reads like something written, not something that happened by accident.

body-cells.prompt: Which of your cells is actually the longest, stretching over 3 feet?
options: A single nerve cell running from the base of your spine to your big toe
A blood vessel cell in your leg
A muscle fiber in your thigh
body-cells.explain: At the other extreme, you could line up about ten red blood cells across the width of a single hair.

body-cells.prompt: When you hold your breath, the urge to gasp comes mainly from your body running out of oxygen.
body-cells.explain: It's mostly your body reacting to waste gas building up, not oxygen running low.

body-voice.prompt: What actually produces the sound of your voice?
options: Two small flaps in your throat slapping together as air passes through
Air vibrating directly against your teeth and lips
A single vocal cord stretching and contracting
body-voice.explain: A child's flaps slap about 285 times a second; an adult man's only about 145 — longer, heavier flaps swing more slowly, making a deeper voice.

body-voice.prompt: A study recording newborn babies' cries in their first days found something surprising. What was it?
options: French and German babies' cries followed different pitch patterns, matching the language they'd heard in the womb
All babies cry with the exact same pitch pattern worldwide
Babies' cries have no pitch pattern until they start babbling
body-voice.explain: French babies' cries mostly rose in pitch; German babies' mostly fell — the tune of language arrived before any words could be spoken.

body-voice.prompt: A whisper is just a very quiet version of your normal voice, using the same vocal flaps.
body-voice.explain: In a whisper, the vocal flaps actually hold still — you're shaping the hiss of moving air instead.

body-hands.prompt: How do your fingers bend and straighten, even though there are no muscles inside the fingers themselves?
options: Muscles in your palm and forearm pull on tendons that run down inside each finger
Small joints inside each finger bend on their own
Blood pressure changes push the fingers into position
body-hands.explain: Every finger movement is worked from a distance, by muscles located elsewhere in your hand and arm.

body-hands.prompt: Why do identical twins, who share the same DNA, still have different fingerprints?
options: The ridges form from how skin buckles randomly in the womb, not purely from DNA instructions
Their fingerprints actually do match exactly
Fingerprints change too much after birth to compare
body-hands.explain: The ridges buckle into place between about weeks 10 and 16 in the womb, and never change after that.

body-hands.prompt: Leaving your little finger out of your grip barely affects your overall hand strength.
body-hands.explain: Measured on a grip meter, leaving out the little finger actually costs about a third of your total grip strength.

body-heat.prompt: The famous "98.6°F" body temperature — is that actually accurate for most people today?
options: Not quite — that figure came from one 1851 doctor's readings, and the average today measures closer to 97.9°F
Yes, it's still exactly accurate for everyone
It was always wrong and has never matched anyone
body-heat.explain: Your own temperature also naturally shifts by about a degree over the course of a day.

body-heat.prompt: Why doesn't sweat cool you down while it's just sitting on your skin?
options: The cooling only happens as sweat evaporates into vapor
Sweat needs to soak fully into the skin first
Cooling happens immediately, but too slowly to notice
body-heat.explain: That's exactly why a muggy, humid day feels so much worse than a dry one — sweat can't evaporate as easily.

body-heat.prompt: A person has actually survived with a measured core body temperature below 57°F, with no heartbeat.
body-heat.explain: Anna Bagenholm was pulled from under river ice at 56.7°F with no heartbeat — and lived.

body-growing.prompt: Why are you measurably taller in the morning than right before bed?
options: The discs in your spine decompress and expand overnight
Your bones actually grow a tiny amount every night
Morning measurements are simply less accurate
body-growing.explain: Most growth hormone is also released during deep sleep, which is why you grow fastest while asleep.

body-growing.prompt: In a growth spurt, which parts of your body typically reach their adult size first?
options: Hands and feet, before arms, legs, and the rest of the body catch up
The head and face, before the rest of the body
The torso, before the arms and legs
body-growing.explain: That's exactly why shoes stop fitting before pants do during a growth spurt.

body-growing.prompt: A baby is born with hard, bony kneecaps, just like an adult's.
body-growing.explain: Babies' kneecaps start as soft cartilage, the same bendy material as the tip of your nose, and harden into bone over several years.

earth-rocks.prompt: On the Mohs hardness scale, what does a mineral's number actually tell you?
options: What it can scratch
How much it weighs
How old it is
earth-rocks.explain: Talc (1) gives way to a fingernail; quartz (7) cuts glass; only another diamond scratches a diamond (10).

earth-rocks.prompt: How did Friedrich Mohs come up with his hardness scale in 1812?
options: He lined up ten minerals by what scratched what
He measured the exact force needed with a machine
He weighed each mineral on a scale
earth-rocks.explain: He never measured a force — he just ranked ten samples and wrote the order down.

earth-rocks.prompt: Ruby and sapphire are actually the same mineral. Which one?
options: Corundum
Quartz
Halite
earth-rocks.explain: A trace of chromium turns corundum red (ruby); iron and titanium turn it blue (sapphire).

earth-rocks.prompt: Why does obsidian have no crystal grain at all?
options: Lava cooled too fast for crystals to form
It's a mix of several different minerals
It's volcanic rock that was never melted
earth-rocks.explain: With no grain to follow, a flake can come to an edge thinner than a steel razor.

earth-rocks.prompt: Table salt is actually a mineral called halite.
earth-rocks.explain: It's soft — about 2 to 2.5 on the hardness scale — which is why it crushes under a spoon.

earth-volcanoes.prompt: What's the real difference between magma and lava?
options: Magma is underground, lava is the same rock once it's out of the vent
Magma is cooler than lava
Lava only comes from explosive volcanoes
earth-volcanoes.explain: Geologists are strict about this — it's the same melted rock with a different address.

earth-volcanoes.prompt: What actually kills people in most volcanic eruptions, according to volcanologists?
options: A pyroclastic flow of hot ash and gas racing downhill
The slow-moving lava itself
Falling ash alone
earth-volcanoes.explain: Most lava creeps slower than walking pace. The pyroclastic flow that hit Pompeii moved faster than 50 mph.

earth-volcanoes.prompt: Nobody has ever seen inside a magma chamber. How do geologists know it's there?
options: Earthquake waves slow down passing through it, and the ground above swells
Drilling equipment has reached one directly
Satellite cameras can see through rock
earth-volcanoes.explain: Instruments read it. No one has ever looked into one.

earth-volcanoes.prompt: Mauna Kea, measured from the sea floor it stands on, is actually taller than Mount Everest.
earth-volcanoes.explain: Most of Mauna Kea is underwater, which is why it doesn't get the title.

earth-volcanoes.prompt: The 1815 eruption of Tambora caused New England farmers to record frost in every month the following year.
earth-volcanoes.explain: 1816 became known as 'the year without a summer' — and 'Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death.'

earth-quakes.prompt: Why is a magnitude 7 earthquake not just "a bit worse" than a magnitude 6?
options: Each whole step releases about 32 times more energy
The scale just counts how many buildings fall
Magnitude only measures how long the shaking lasts
earth-quakes.explain: It would take roughly 32 sixes added together to equal the energy of one seven.

earth-quakes.prompt: How do scientists know what's happening at the Earth's core, since no one has ever been there?
options: They work it out from how earthquake waves bend, slow, and stop
Deep drilling has reached the core directly
Heat sensors buried underground measure it
earth-quakes.explain: Sideways waves can't travel through liquid and vanish partway down — that's why the outer core is reasoned to be molten.

earth-quakes.prompt: What actually causes the two different kinds of shaking wave in one earthquake?
options: Both waves start at the same spot at the same moment, but travel at different speeds
Each wave comes from a separate, smaller earthquake
One wave is caused by the quake, the other by the tsunami
earth-quakes.explain: The fast P wave arrives first; the slower, more damaging S wave lags behind — measuring the gap tells you how far away the quake was.

earth-quakes.prompt: The strongest earthquake ever measured, in Chile in 1960, was a magnitude 9.5.
earth-quakes.explain: The shaking lasted about ten minutes, and the tsunami it caused was still killing people in Hawaii and Japan a day later.

earth-quakes.prompt: Earth's tectonic plates drift at roughly the speed your fingernails grow.
earth-quakes.explain: That's about one to four inches a year, measured by GPS receivers bolted to bedrock.

earth-water.prompt: What's actually at the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the ocean's deepest known point?
options: Water pressing in at over a thousand times surface pressure
Nothing — no one has ever measured it directly
A pressure about the same as at sea level
earth-water.explain: About eight tons on every square inch — enough to crush anything with air inside it.

earth-water.prompt: Of all the fresh water on Earth, where is most of it actually locked up?
options: As ice
In lakes and rivers
Underground
earth-water.explain: Nearly 69 percent of fresh water is ice; lakes and rivers get the leftovers — well under one percent of all fresh water.

earth-water.prompt: Scientists are confident ocean trenches form where one slab of sea floor bends under another. What's that explanation actually based on?
options: The pattern of earthquakes lining up along a slanting sheet underground
Divers who have measured the bending slab directly
Core samples pulled up from the trench floor
earth-water.explain: The depth of a trench is measured; how it formed is worked out from where the quakes happen, which is a different kind of claim.

earth-water.prompt: The Amazon River pours more fresh water into the ocean than any other river on Earth.
earth-water.explain: About five times the Congo and twelve times the Mississippi — roughly a fifth of all river water reaching the sea.

earth-water.prompt: More of the Moon's surface has been mapped in detail than the bottom of Earth's own ocean.
earth-water.explain: Only about 29 percent of the sea floor has been mapped in detail with modern sonar.

earth-weather.prompt: Why is the air inside a lightning bolt hotter than the surface of the sun?
options: Air is a terrible conductor, and resisting the current is what dumps the heat
Lightning bolts are made of fire
The sun is actually cooler than most people think
earth-weather.explain: The same reason a thin wire glows orange inside a toaster — about 50,000°F, roughly five times the sun's surface.

earth-weather.prompt: What's the old explanation for a hailstone's onion-like layers, and why is it wrong?
options: One layer per loop through the storm — but nobody can track a hailstone's path inside a cloud
The layers form after the hailstone lands
Hailstones don't actually have layers
earth-weather.explain: The layers are read as patches of different temperature and wetness, mostly from one pass across the updraft, not repeated loops.

earth-weather.prompt: How can you tell roughly how far away a lightning strike was?
options: Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, then divide by five
Count how many seconds the thunder itself lasts
Compare how bright the flash looked
earth-weather.explain: Light arrives almost instantly; sound crawls at about one mile every five seconds.

earth-weather.prompt: A single ordinary puffy cloud can carry over a million pounds of water.
earth-weather.explain: It stays up because the water is chopped into droplets far too small to fall quickly.

earth-weather.prompt: No two snowflakes have ever actually been proven to be completely unique.
earth-weather.explain: Nobody has compared every snowflake that's ever fallen — simple small crystals actually do look identical.

earth-caves.prompt: How do geologists actually know how caves form, since nobody has ever watched one form?
options: They can measure that water leaving cave springs is carrying dissolved limestone right now
Someone has watched a small cave form in a lab
Ancient written records describe it happening
earth-caves.explain: Rain picks up carbon dioxide, becomes a weak acid, and eats limestone — the chemistry is measured even though the forming isn't observed.

earth-caves.prompt: What's the easy trick for remembering stalactites from stalagmites?
options: C is for ceiling, G is for ground
Stalactites are always bigger
Stalagmites only form in warm caves
earth-caves.explain: They usually come as a matched pair, since one drip builds both.

earth-caves.prompt: What proved a canyon as deep as the Grand Canyon could be cut in a single day?
options: A 1982 flood at Mount St. Helens that cut a riverbed overnight
Satellite photos taken a year apart
A team that measured the Grand Canyon forming in real time
earth-caves.explain: Ten miles below the crater, the riverbed dropped an average of 9 feet overnight — people watched this one happen.

earth-caves.prompt: Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave, and its length was measured by volunteers crawling it with tape measures.
earth-caves.explain: It holds 426 miles of mapped passage — no other known cave comes close.

earth-caves.prompt: Movile Cave in Romania is full of animals that depend on sunlight to survive.
earth-caves.explain: Nothing down there runs on sunlight — the bottom of the food chain is bacteria living on hydrogen sulfide and methane.

earth-ice.prompt: Why does only about a tenth of an iceberg stick up above the water?
options: Ice is only slightly less dense than seawater, so it sinks until it displaces its own weight
Icebergs are hollow underneath
The underwater part is a different, heavier kind of ice
earth-ice.explain: For the same amount of space, ice is roughly nine-tenths as heavy as seawater.

earth-ice.prompt: Why doesn't melting floating sea ice raise sea level, while melting land ice does?
options: Floating ice is already displacing its own weight in water; land ice isn't in the ocean yet
Sea ice melts into a different, lighter kind of water
Land ice is actually much colder
earth-ice.explain: An ice cube melting in a full glass doesn't overflow it — but ice melting on a saucer and then poured in does.

earth-ice.prompt: Why are at the South Pole, day and night each six months long?
options: The sun circles the sky without setting for half the year, then stays down the other half
It's always completely dark there
The sun rises and sets normally, just more slowly
earth-ice.explain: The sun rises around late September, circles for six months, then sets around late March.

earth-ice.prompt: Snow looks white and glacier ice looks blue, even though both are made of the exact same clear substance.
earth-ice.explain: Snow's tiny surfaces bounce every color straight back; thick solid ice absorbs reds and lets blue through.

earth-sky.prompt: Why does the same side of the Moon always face Earth?
options: It spins at exactly the same rate it orbits us
It doesn't spin at all
It's locked in place by Earth's gravity with no motion
earth-sky.explain: One turn per orbit, about 27 days — if it stopped spinning, we'd start seeing every side.

earth-sky.prompt: What actually causes most coasts to get two high tides a day instead of one?
options: The Moon's pull bulges the ocean on the near side AND the far side, and Earth turns through both
The Sun and Moon pull in opposite directions twice a day
Ocean currents push water back and forth
earth-sky.explain: On the far side, water is pulled least and gets left behind — Earth rotates through both bulges daily.

earth-sky.prompt: Why do Earth's seasons happen, if we're actually closest to the sun in January?
options: Earth's 23.4-degree axis tilt, not distance from the sun
The sun gets hotter and cooler throughout the year
Clouds block more sunlight in winter
earth-sky.explain: Australia has summer while Canada has winter — same planet, same distance, same day.

earth-sky.prompt: The sun and moon look almost the same size in our sky purely by coincidence of their size and distance canceling out.
earth-sky.explain: The sun is about 400 times wider than the moon, and also about 400 times farther away.

earth-sky.prompt: Nobody saw the far side of the Moon until a spacecraft photographed it in 1959.
earth-sky.explain: A Soviet probe, Luna 3, sent back the first photos — and the far side turned out to be covered in craters.

micro-cell.prompt: Why did Robert Hooke call the tiny boxes he saw in cork "cells" in 1665?
options: They reminded him of the small rooms monks slept in
He named them after his own last name
A colleague suggested the word
micro-cell.explain: The name stuck ever since, from his bestselling book of drawings, Micrographia.

micro-cell.prompt: How do scientists know you're made of roughly 30 trillion cells, since nobody has ever counted them one by one?
options: By weighing organs and working out the typical size and weight of each kind of cell
By scanning the whole body with a special camera
It's an old number nobody has ever questioned
micro-cell.explain: This corrected figure, published in 2016, replaced an older guess that had gone unchecked for decades and was several times too big.

micro-cell.prompt: What do the hundreds of bean-shaped parts inside almost every cell actually do?
options: Release energy from food
Store the cell's DNA
Help the cell move
micro-cell.explain: They're called mitochondria — a hardworking heart muscle cell can be a third mitochondria by volume.

micro-cell.prompt: If you stretched out the DNA from just one of your cells, it would measure about 6 feet long.
micro-cell.explain: It fits inside the tiny cell because it's wound around protein spools and coiled again and again.

micro-bacteria.prompt: For decades, people repeated the claim that bacteria outnumber your own cells ten to one. What happened when someone actually checked?
options: The real ratio turned out to be closer to one to one
The claim turned out to be exactly right
Bacteria turned out to outnumber cells by a hundred to one
micro-bacteria.explain: The ten-to-one figure came from a rough 1972 estimate that was simply never properly measured.

micro-bacteria.prompt: Why do doctors insist you finish an entire course of antibiotics, even once you feel better?
options: A few surviving bacteria can breed, and their offspring also survive the drug
Stopping early wastes the unused medicine
It takes that long for the drug to enter your bloodstream
micro-bacteria.explain: This has actually been filmed in laboratories — bacteria creeping into bands of stronger and stronger drug.

micro-bacteria.prompt: A heat-tolerant bacterium found in a Yellowstone hot spring turned out to be useful for what?
options: A heat-proof copying enzyme now used in DNA tests worldwide
Making bread rise faster
Producing modern antibiotics
micro-bacteria.explain: Every DNA test you've heard of depends on a microbe first found in a hot pool in Wyoming.

micro-bacteria.prompt: Most of the thousands of kinds of bacteria living on your skin and in your gut are actually trying to make you sick.
micro-bacteria.explain: Only a small handful cause disease — most are doing nothing to you, and plenty are useful.

micro-virus.prompt: Why is it genuinely debated whether a virus counts as "alive"?
options: It can't eat, grow, or copy itself — it only does anything once inside a living cell
All scientists agree it's definitely alive
It's too small to study closely enough to tell
micro-virus.explain: The usual tests for life simply give contradictory answers for a virus — it's an open question, not a trick one.

micro-virus.prompt: Why won't antibiotics do anything to help a cold?
options: Antibiotics attack machinery that bacteria have and viruses don't
Colds are too mild for antibiotics to bother with
Antibiotics only work on old infections
micro-virus.explain: Taking antibiotics for a virus can't help, and makes resistant bacteria more likely.

micro-virus.prompt: How did Edward Jenner create the first vaccine in 1796?
options: He noticed milkmaids who'd had cowpox didn't catch smallpox, then tested the idea on a boy
He isolated the smallpox virus in a laboratory
He studied old medical records from past outbreaks
micro-virus.explain: Smallpox is the only human disease ever wiped out — declared gone in 1980.

micro-virus.prompt: There's no single cure for "the common cold" because there's no single virus that causes it.
micro-virus.explain: More than two hundred different viruses produce the same symptoms — beating one still leaves 199 others.

micro-fungi.prompt: What actually causes bread dough to rise?
options: Yeast eating sugar and giving off carbon dioxide gas, trapped in bubbles
Air getting whipped into the dough while kneading
Heat from the oven expanding the dough
micro-fungi.explain: Every hole in a slice of bread is literally a bubble of yeast breath.

micro-fungi.prompt: Where does mold actually come from when it appears on old bread?
options: It's already floating in the air as spores, waiting for something damp
It's carried onto the bread by insects
It grows spontaneously from the bread itself
micro-fungi.explain: Leaving bread out isn't "catching" mold — you're simply providing a damp home for spores already in the air.

micro-fungi.prompt: What did Alexander Fleming actually notice in 1928 that led to penicillin?
options: Bacteria were dead in a clear ring around mold on a dish he'd left out
A patient recovered unexpectedly fast from an infection
Mold samples under a microscope looked unusual
micro-fungi.explain: It took another twelve years and a different team to turn that observation into a usable drug.

micro-fungi.prompt: A single fungus found in an Oregon forest has been shown to be one organism spread across 3.4 square miles underground.
micro-fungi.explain: It was mapped by testing samples from all over the forest to see which ones were genetically the same individual.

micro-pond.prompt: How does an amoeba move, since it has no legs, fins, or fixed shape at all?
options: It pours part of itself forward and lets the rest follow
It uses tiny hair-like structures to swim
It rolls like a ball through the water
micro-pond.explain: It eats the same way — flowing around something until it's completely surrounded, with no mouth at all.

micro-pond.prompt: What are diatoms, the single-celled organisms Victorian scientists used to test their microscope lenses?
options: Cells that build themselves glass boxes with finely patterned lids
Bacteria that glow in the dark
The fastest-swimming creatures in pond water
micro-pond.explain: The patterns are so fine and regular that when diatoms die, their shells pile up as diatomaceous earth.

micro-pond.prompt: A jar of pond water left on a windowsill for a week will actually have MORE living things in it than the day you collected it.
micro-pond.explain: Any still water with good light can support a growing population — you've essentially made a small pond.

micro-helpers.prompt: What do the bacteria living in your large intestine actually do for you?
options: Break down fiber you can't digest, and make vitamin K your blood needs to clot
Nothing — they just live there without affecting you
Protect you from catching colds
micro-helpers.explain: People on long courses of antibiotics sometimes need extra vitamin K for exactly this reason.

micro-helpers.prompt: What's actually happening in the little lumps on the roots of a pea or clover plant?
options: Bacteria there pull nitrogen from the air and trade it to the plant for sugar
The plant stores extra water there
Insects lay their eggs in those lumps
micro-helpers.explain: It's a genuine trade — the bacteria get fed, and the plant gets natural fertilizer.

micro-helpers.prompt: Without fungi and bacteria breaking down dead leaves and wood, the ground would eventually be buried meters deep in them.
micro-helpers.explain: All that material would stay locked up in what had already lived, and nothing new could grow.

micro-clean.prompt: In 1847, what did Ignaz Semmelweis discover was killing new mothers in one hospital ward far more than another?
options: Doctors weren't washing their hands after working with the dead
The midwives' ward had better equipment
One ward used dirtier bed linens
micro-clean.explain: He was ignored and mocked at the time — germs hadn't been demonstrated yet, so nobody could see what he was talking about.

micro-clean.prompt: How does soap actually destroy germs, rather than "poisoning" them?
options: One end of the soap molecule grips grease, the other grips water, lifting germs off and down the drain
It changes the pH of the skin so germs can't survive
It coats your skin in a protective barrier
micro-clean.explain: A virus with a fatty coat simply falls apart when soap gets to it.

micro-clean.prompt: Why does a fever actually happen when you get sick?
options: Your own body raises its temperature on purpose, since most germs grow worse in heat
The germ itself raises your body temperature as a side effect
It's a sign your immune system has failed
micro-clean.explain: A mild fever is a weapon your body is using, not damage being done.

micro-clean.prompt: A refrigerator actually kills the bacteria in food, the same way cooking does.
micro-clean.explain: A fridge only slows bacteria down — it takes days instead of hours for them to reach harmful numbers, and they start multiplying again once thawed.

micro-scope.prompt: Why couldn't viruses be seen by anyone until the 1930s, no matter how good their microscope was?
options: Any light microscope has a hard size limit, since objects smaller than light waves can't be seen that way
Nobody had thought to look for anything that small before
Viruses used to be much larger than they are today
micro-scope.explain: That limit comes from the behavior of light itself, not from trying better lenses — it's why the electron microscope was needed.

micro-scope.prompt: What's the trade-off of using an electron microscope to see something as small as a virus?
options: It works in a vacuum, so nothing being looked at can be alive or moving
It can only see things that are already dead and decayed
It only works on metal objects
micro-scope.explain: You get to see the virus, but you never get to see it moving.

micro-scope.prompt: A single drop of water, held up over a printed page, actually works as a simple magnifying lens.
micro-scope.explain: It works on the same principle as the tiny glass bead Van Leeuwenhoek used to first see a bacterium.

physical-forces.prompt: On the moon, astronauts dropped a hammer and a feather together. What happened?
options: They hit the ground at the same time
The hammer landed first, just like on Earth
The feather floated and never landed
physical-forces.explain: With no air in the way, there's nothing to slow the feather down — Galileo argued this but could never prove it on Earth.

physical-forces.prompt: Why does a rocket actually move forward in empty space, where there's nothing to push against?
options: It throws gas out the back, and the gas pushes the rocket forward
It pushes against the air behind it
Gravity pulls it forward
physical-forces.explain: Every push comes with an equal push the other way — rockets work better in space, where nothing is in the way.

physical-forces.prompt: A moving object will keep moving forever in a straight line unless something pushes or pulls on it.
physical-forces.explain: You rarely see this on Earth because friction and air resistance are always pushing back — it shows clearly on ice or in space.

physical-energy.prompt: How does the number on a cereal box's "Calories" label actually get measured?
options: The food is burned in a sealed chamber, and scientists measure how much the surrounding water heats up
It's estimated by comparing the food to similar foods
A machine scans the food's chemical ingredients
physical-energy.explain: The device is called a bomb calorimeter — it's exactly as dramatic as it sounds.

physical-energy.prompt: What makes a bicycle the most energy-efficient way for a person to travel, compared to walking?
options: Almost no energy is wasted holding you up
Bicycles use electricity instead of muscle power
Walking requires more oxygen overall
physical-energy.explain: Measured by energy used per pound carried per mile, walking uses about three times as much as cycling.

physical-energy.prompt: Scientists have found cases where energy actually appears out of nowhere or vanishes completely.
physical-energy.explain: Nobody has ever seen an exception — it's the most tested idea in physics, even though it can't be proven for every event in the universe.

physical-light.prompt: Why is the sky blue during the day but red at sunset?
options: Air scatters blue light more than red; at sunset light travels through far more air, scattering the blue away entirely
The sun itself changes color at sunset
Clouds filter out different colors at different times
physical-light.explain: Short wavelengths like blue bounce around the sky; red comes straight through.

physical-light.prompt: What did Newton prove by putting a SECOND prism in the path of light that a first prism had already split into colors?
options: That the colors recombine back into white light
That each color is actually a separate kind of light
That prisms only work with sunlight
physical-light.explain: He did the part people forget — showing the split was reversible, not that he'd created new colors.

physical-light.prompt: Mixing red, green, and blue light together makes white light, the same way mixing red, green, and blue paint does.
physical-light.explain: Mixing light and mixing paint are opposites — mixed paint makes muddy brown, because each paint takes colors away instead of adding them.

physical-sound.prompt: What does a classic classroom experiment with a ringing alarm inside a jar prove, once the air is pumped out?
options: Sound needs something to travel through — space is truly silent
Sound gets louder in a vacuum
The alarm stops working without air
physical-sound.explain: The ringing fades to nothing even though you can still see the hammer moving — the experiment is over 300 years old.

physical-sound.prompt: How can you measure how far away a thunderstorm is, using nothing but your own senses?
options: Time the gap between the lightning flash and the thunder, since light arrives instantly but sound takes time
Count how loud the thunder sounds
Watch how fast the clouds are moving
physical-sound.explain: Sound moves about a mile every five seconds through air — light is effectively instant by comparison.

physical-sound.prompt: A wine glass can actually be shattered just by someone singing the right note at it.
physical-sound.explain: Everything has a note it prefers to vibrate at — sing that note at it and it starts vibrating on its own.

physical-heat.prompt: Does a refrigerator actually create cold air?
options: No — it removes heat from the inside and dumps it out the back
Yes — it generates cold air with a special chemical
No — it just insulates the inside from outside heat
physical-heat.explain: Heat only ever moves from hotter to colder — put your hand behind a fridge and feel the heat it's dumping out.

physical-heat.prompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon sitting on the same counter are the exact same temperature. Why does the metal one feel colder?
options: Metal carries heat away from your skin faster — your skin senses that, not the actual temperature
The metal spoon is always a few degrees colder
Wood somehow generates its own heat
physical-heat.explain: Your skin doesn't measure temperature directly — it measures how quickly heat is leaving your finger.

physical-heat.prompt: Almost every substance shrinks when it freezes — water is one of the rare exceptions that expands instead.
physical-heat.explain: Water expands by about nine percent when it freezes, which is why ice floats and ponds freeze from the top down.

physical-electric.prompt: Why does breaking an electrical circuit anywhere stop the whole thing from working?
options: Electricity only flows around a complete, unbroken loop
Electricity needs a battery to restart after any gap
Switches only block part of the current
physical-electric.explain: That's exactly what a switch is — and why one dead bulb used to kill a whole string of old Christmas lights.

physical-electric.prompt: How do scientists know how much electric current is flowing through a wire, since electrons are far too small to see?
options: A current pushes a magnet by a measurable amount, and that's what an ammeter reads
They count the electrons directly with a microscope
They weigh the wire before and after
physical-electric.explain: Nobody has ever watched an electron move down a wire — the effect is measured, and the amount is worked out from it.

physical-electric.prompt: Pure, completely clean water actually conducts electricity poorly — it's the salt and minerals dissolved in real water that make it dangerous.
physical-electric.explain: The rule is never really about water itself — it's about what's dissolved in it, including in your own body.

physical-magnets.prompt: If you snap a bar magnet in half, what do you get?
options: Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south end
A separate north piece and south piece
A magnet that no longer has any poles
physical-magnets.explain: You cannot get a single pole on its own, no matter how many times you break a magnet apart.

physical-magnets.prompt: What's the quickest way to turn an iron nail into a magnet?
options: Wrap wire around it and connect a battery
Rub it against another piece of iron for a long time
Leave it outside in a storm
physical-magnets.explain: Electricity and magnetism are the same force wearing different hats — disconnect the battery and the magnetism stops.

physical-magnets.prompt: A compass needle points directly at the Earth's true North Pole.
physical-magnets.explain: It points at the magnetic pole instead, which can be tens of degrees off depending where you're standing — and it's slowly moving toward Siberia.

physical-matter.prompt: Why does water boil at a lower temperature in a mountain city like Denver than at sea level?
options: There's less air pressure pushing down on it at higher altitude
Mountain water is naturally purer
Cold mountain air cools the water as it boils
physical-matter.explain: Denver's water boils at about 202°F instead of 212°F — which is why food takes longer to cook there.

physical-matter.prompt: A massive steel ship floats, but a small steel bolt sinks. Why?
options: Floating depends on how heavy something is for its size, not its total weight
Ships are made of a different, lighter metal
The ocean only supports large objects
physical-matter.explain: Most of a steel ship's volume is actually air — a solid steel bolt has no such space inside it.

physical-matter.prompt: Scientists have taken a real photograph of individual atoms by shining a very bright light on them.
physical-matter.explain: Atoms are smaller than light waves, so no light-based microscope can show one — the images come from dragging an extremely fine needle across a surface instead.

world-middle.prompt: In 1086, the King of England ordered a survey so detailed people nicknamed it after Judgment Day. What did it record?
options: Who owned what, down to individual plows, mills, and pigs
Only the largest estates and castles
How much tax each town owed
world-middle.explain: The Domesday Book fills two volumes — there was no appealing what it said you owned.

world-middle.prompt: Where does the word "masterpiece" actually come from?
options: A medieval guild apprentice's qualifying piece of work, judged before he could become a master craftsman
A term for the greatest artwork of an era
A piece commissioned by a king
world-middle.explain: It originally meant a qualifying test, not a great work of art.

world-middle.prompt: The Bayeux Tapestry is actually woven cloth, exactly like other tapestries of its time.
