world-middle.explain: It's embroidery — wool thread stitched onto linen in eight colors, running 230 feet long.

world-voyages.prompt: How many of Ferdinand Magellan's roughly 270 original crew actually completed the voyage around the world?
options: Eighteen, on one ship, without Magellan himself
All five ships returned safely
About half the original crew
world-voyages.explain: Magellan was killed in the Philippines — Juan Sebastián Elcano finished the voyage in his place.

world-voyages.prompt: How did Polynesian navigators cross thousands of miles of open Pacific Ocean with no instruments?
options: By reading stars, swells, cloud shapes, and bird flight paths
By following established sea routes marked with buoys
By using early compasses made from magnetized stone
world-voyages.explain: In 1976 a crew successfully sailed this way from Hawaii to Tahiti, though they had to bring in a navigator from Micronesia since the knowledge had been lost in Hawaii.

world-voyages.prompt: A naval surgeon in 1747 proved citrus fruit cured scurvy by testing different remedies on groups of sick sailors.
world-voyages.explain: It's one of the first properly controlled trials ever run — though the navy took over forty years to act on the results.

world-printing.prompt: What was Gutenberg's real breakthrough invention — more important than the printing press itself?
options: A mold that could quickly cast thousands of identical metal letters
A new type of paper
A faster way to bind pages into books
world-printing.explain: The metal alloy was soft enough to cast and hard enough to print — pages came out so even, people doubted they weren't handwritten.

world-printing.prompt: Where was paper actually invented, long before it reached Europe?
options: China
Egypt
Baghdad
world-printing.explain: It took about a thousand years to travel west along the Silk Road — before that, Europeans wrote on animal skin.

world-printing.prompt: The printing press was an entirely new invention, built from scratch with no earlier machine to base it on.
world-printing.explain: The press itself was borrowed from big screw presses that wine and olive growers had used for centuries.

world-discovery.prompt: What did Evangelista Torricelli accidentally invent by turning a mercury-filled tube upside down in a dish?
options: The first barometer, by discovering that air itself has weight
The first clock accurate enough for sea travel
A way to measure temperature
world-discovery.explain: The mercury column dropped and stopped at a fixed height — something was holding it up, and that something was the weight of the air.

world-discovery.prompt: What was the Royal Society's core principle, captured in its Latin motto?
options: Take nobody's word for it — do the experiment in front of witnesses, and publish even the failures
Knowledge should be kept among scholars only
Only royalty could fund scientific research
world-discovery.explain: Publishing failures honestly is the part later ages have found hardest to keep up.

world-discovery.prompt: John Harrison spent decades trying to build a clock accurate enough to use at sea, since a clock that lost even a few seconds a day could put a ship miles off course.
world-discovery.explain: Every four seconds of error meant being a mile out of position — his winning design was a watch about 5 inches across.

world-builders.prompt: Can the Great Wall of China actually be seen from space with the naked eye, as often claimed?
options: No — astronauts have repeatedly said it can't, and photographs back them up
Yes, it's the only human structure visible from orbit
Only from very low orbit, not from the moon
world-builders.explain: Highways and airport runways are actually much easier to spot, since they're wider and a different color than the ground around them.

world-builders.prompt: How were the great carved facades at Petra actually built into the sandstone cliff?
options: Carvers started at the top and worked downward, needing no scaffolding
Blocks were carved separately and assembled against the cliff
Workers tunneled in from behind the cliff face
world-builders.explain: They cut away the rock beneath their own feet as they went — unfinished tombs still show where work stopped partway down.

world-builders.prompt: Laser surveys of the jungle around Angkor Wat revealed an entire forgotten city with roads and reservoirs.
world-builders.explain: The lasers fired through gaps in the forest canopy, mapping streets nobody had walked on for centuries.

world-faroff.prompt: How were Timbuktu's hundreds of thousands of manuscripts saved when the city was threatened?
options: Librarians smuggled them out in rice sacks and fishing boats
They were buried underground for protection
They were copied and sent to European museums
world-faroff.explain: The manuscripts cover astronomy, medicine, law, and mathematics — kept by families for generations.

world-faroff.prompt: What was the Silk Road actually like, despite its name suggesting a single path?
options: A shifting web of routes where goods were handed town to town, with almost nobody traveling the whole length
One well-defined road maintained by multiple empires
A sea route primarily used for trading silk
world-faroff.explain: Paper, gunpowder, printing, and disease all spread this way too — very little silk itself reached the far end.

world-faroff.prompt: The Inca kept detailed numerical records without any system of writing, using knotted cords called quipu.
world-faroff.explain: The color, knot type, and position on the cord all carried meaning — whether they recorded words too is still not settled.

world-medicine.prompt: Before 1846, how was surgery typically performed?
options: On patients who were awake and held down, as fast as the surgeon could work
With early forms of anesthesia already in common use
Only as a last resort, rarely attempted
world-medicine.explain: That October, a dentist gave a patient ether in Boston, and the surgeon afterward said, 'gentlemen, this is no humbug.'

world-medicine.prompt: What made Florence Nightingale's work during the war so effective at changing military medical policy?
options: She invented a diagram showing far more soldiers died of disease than of wounds
She personally treated more patients than any other nurse
She wrote detailed letters home describing conditions
world-medicine.explain: Her circular chart laid deaths out month by month, and she put it directly in front of the people who could act on it.

world-medicine.prompt: Smallpox is the only human disease ever completely wiped out worldwide.
world-medicine.explain: The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977 — it worked because the virus only lives in people, and the rash makes it easy to spot and contain.

world-modern.prompt: When Marconi claimed to receive the first transatlantic radio signal in 1901, why were physicists skeptical?
options: Radio waves were thought to travel in straight lines, and the curve of the Earth should have blocked the signal
They didn't believe radio waves existed at all
The distance was thought to be too far for any signal
world-modern.explain: He turned out to be right for a reason nobody knew yet — the waves bounce off a layer high in the atmosphere.

world-modern.prompt: What invention made shipping goods across the ocean dramatically cheaper, starting in 1956?
options: The standardized steel shipping container
Larger cargo ships with bigger holds
Faster-loading cranes at ports
world-modern.explain: Loading a ship by hand once cost several dollars a ton — by container it fell to a few cents.

world-modern.prompt: GPS satellites need their onboard clocks specially corrected, because time actually runs at a slightly different rate in orbit.
world-modern.explain: Left uncorrected, your phone's calculated position would drift by about 6 miles a day.
